collection: NECO Health Education vector-control observation practice
note: Original structured practice using mock inspection records. NECO lists Test of Practical; exact task specifications remain open. Academic review pending.

questions.subject: Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Interpret mock inspection observations and explain how barrier and vector-control measures differ.
questions.prompt: A mock dormitory inspection records two sleeping spaces. Space A has an insecticide-treated net hanging over the bed, with one edge raised above the mattress. Space B has an intact net enclosing the bed, but its label is missing. Identify a barrier fault at A and explain what the observer can and cannot conclude about B.
questions.answer: A has an opening that can let mosquitoes enter the sleeping space. B appears to have a continuous physical barrier, but the inspection does not establish whether it is insecticide-treated.
questions.explanation: Barrier condition can be observed directly. Treatment status needs other evidence, such as a label or supply record.

markingGuide.description: Explain what can be observed about B.
Identify treatment status as unverified and give suitable confirming evidence.

questions.subject: Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Interpret mock inspection observations and explain how barrier and vector-control measures differ.
questions.prompt: A display labels specimen A as an insecticide-treated bed net and specimen B as a drawing of a trained team applying indoor residual spray to interior walls. For each, identify where the intervention acts and describe one difference in how protection is delivered.
questions.answer: A is used around a sleeping space and provides a barrier with insecticide on the net. B treats indoor resting surfaces so susceptible mosquitoes contacting those surfaces are exposed.
questions.explanation: Compare a personal sleeping-space intervention with a professionally applied treatment of indoor surfaces.

markingGuide.description: Identify where the net is used.
Identify the treated surfaces in B.
Explain one mechanism difference between the methods.

questions.subject: Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Interpret mock inspection observations and explain how barrier and vector-control measures differ.
questions.prompt: In a simulated inspection of 24 sleeping places, 20 had nets assigned, 16 of the assigned nets were hung and 12 of the hung nets were recorded as closed around the bed. A report claims 20 sleeping places were observed with a closed net. Correct the claim and give one further observation needed to assess actual use.
questions.answer: Only 12 of 24 were recorded with closed nets. Allocation is an inventory measure. To assess use, record whether people actually sleep under the nets during the period being assessed.
questions.explanation: Use the count for the reported condition. An observed setup is different from verified use.

markingGuide.description: Use 12 as the count meeting the observed condition.
Distinguish allocation, setup and observed closure.
Specify an observation that would help assess use.

questions.subject: Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Interpret observation records, assess sampling limitations and propose checks for breeding-site controls.
questions.prompt: A mock grounds survey records rainwater in an old tyre, an empty dry bucket and a sealed water-storage drum. Identify which location has the clearest immediate sign of a potential breeding site. Give a control measure for that location and an observation that would verify the measure afterwards.
questions.answer: The tyre contains standing water. Empty it safely and store it under cover or remove it through an appropriate disposal route. Recheck after rain to see whether water still collects.
questions.explanation: The observation identifies a potential site. The follow-up checks whether the intervention prevents water from accumulating again.

markingGuide.description: Select the tyre using the observed water.
Propose a feasible way to stop repeat accumulation.
Give a follow-up observation tied to that control.

questions.subject: Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Interpret observation records, assess sampling limitations and propose checks for breeding-site controls.
questions.prompt: Two student teams report potential breeding sites. Team A found six water-holding containers after inspecting 12 compounds. Team B found eight after inspecting 40. Compare the rates per inspected compound and explain why these figures alone cannot establish which area has more mosquito breeding.
questions.answer: Team A found 0.5 containers per compound and Team B found 0.2. The inspection counted water-holding containers, without confirming larvae or establishing that the inspected compounds represent their areas.
questions.explanation: Compare rates using each team’s denominator. Separate a potential-site indicator from direct evidence of breeding.

markingGuide.description: Compare the rates in the correct direction.
Explain an evidence limitation and name an observation or sampling improvement.

questions.subject: Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Interpret observation records, assess sampling limitations and propose checks for breeding-site controls.
questions.prompt: A school introduces covered lids for its water drums. Design a four-week observation sheet to check whether the lids stay in place. Identify what would count as a failed inspection and how you would keep results comparable across weeks.
questions.answer: Use one row per drum per inspection, with drum ID, date, lid condition and whether it fits securely. Count missing, open or ill-fitting lids as failures. Revisit the same drums on a consistent schedule and apply the same scoring rules.
questions.explanation: A useful observation sheet identifies the units checked, defines failures consistently and lets the school compare results over time.

markingGuide.description: Include an identifier and observation date.
Record the condition or fit of the lid.
Use the same drums and rules or explain how changes are recorded.
